package_info.package_manager: N/A (delivered via email attachment, not a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The HTML file is specifically crafted to exploit the Windows Search URI protocol (search-ms:), redirecting users to attacker-controlled remote servers via search queries. This enables the attacker to execute unauthorized code, deliver malware payloads, and exfiltrate data by abusing Windows Search and WebDAV, all under the guise of a legitimate document. The attack leverages social engineering and OS-level protocol abuse to bypass traditional email security controls.

execution_context.trigger: user interaction (opening HTML attachment in email client or browser)
execution_context.file_location: malicious HTML file inside zipped email attachment

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the HTML attachment, the browser immediately executes a meta refresh, which triggers the Windows Search URI protocol, causing Windows Explorer to perform a search for files named 'INVOICE' in the specified local directory, resulting in the display of potentially malicious or misleading files to the user.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a meta refresh tag to invoke the search-ms: URI is highly unusual and enables the HTML file to trigger OS-level search operations, which can be abused to lure users into interacting with attacker-controlled content.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Standard HTML documents are not expected to invoke Windows Search or interact with the local file system via custom URI schemes, especially when delivered as unsolicited email attachments.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise environments may use custom URI schemes for internal tools, but these are typically deployed in trusted, controlled contexts—not in unsolicited or externally sourced email attachments.
key_indicators: Immediate redirection via <meta http-equiv="refresh"> to a search-ms: URI
Abuse of search-ms: protocol to trigger Windows Explorer actions
Targeting of specific file names (e.g., 'INVOICE') to entice user interaction
Redirection to OS-level protocol from within an HTML file

execution_context.trigger: user interaction (clicking a link in the HTML file)
execution_context.file_location: malicious HTML file inside zipped email attachment

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user clicks the link in the HTML file, the browser or email client invokes the search-ms: URI protocol, causing Windows Explorer to perform a search for 'INVOICE' files in a remote WebDAV share controlled by the attacker, resulting in attacker-hosted files being displayed as if they are local resources.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: HTML links should not invoke Windows Search on remote UNC paths, especially those pointing to attacker-controlled WebDAV shares, as this can be used to deliver malware or harvest credentials.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal HTML links are expected to point to web resources (http/https), not to local or remote file system searches via OS-level protocols, particularly in the context of email attachments.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Internal documentation or enterprise tools may use search-ms: links for productivity, but these are not distributed via unsolicited email attachments and do not target remote, untrusted shares.
key_indicators: search-ms: URI with remote UNC path (e.g., \\malicious-server\share)
Display name set to mimic legitimate folders (e.g., 'Downloads')
Social engineering lure in link text (e.g., 'Click here to view your invoice')
Invocation of Windows Explorer search on attacker-controlled network shares

execution_context.file_location: Windows Registry (via command line or script execution)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After successful exploitation, the attacker executes a command to forcibly delete the Windows Search URI protocol handler from the registry, removing evidence of the attack and preventing further use or detection of the search-ms: protocol.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting protocol handlers from the registry is a strong indicator of anti-forensic or persistence techniques, as it disrupts normal system functionality and can hide traces of exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software rarely removes protocol handlers without explicit user consent, and such actions are not part of normal document or email attachment handling.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may remove unused or vulnerable protocols for system hardening, but this is done through controlled processes, not as part of document-driven workflows.
key_indicators: Registry deletion of search-ms protocol handler (HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\search-ms)
Use of /f flag for forced deletion without user confirmation
Execution of registry modification commands post-exploitation

attack_chain.action: User receives a phishing email containing a zipped HTML attachment designed to appear as a legitimate document (e.g., invoice).
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens the HTML file, initiating the attack sequence.

attack_chain.action: HTML file executes a meta refresh or presents a clickable link that triggers the Windows Search URI protocol (search-ms:), causing Windows Explorer to perform a search.
attack_chain.leads_to: Windows Explorer performs a search, potentially accessing attacker-controlled remote files.

attack_chain.action: Windows Explorer connects to a remote WebDAV share specified in the search-ms: URI, displaying attacker-controlled files as if they are local resources.
attack_chain.leads_to: User may execute or open malicious files, leading to malware infection or credential theft.

attack_chain.action: Attacker removes the Windows Search protocol handler from the registry to cover tracks and prevent further detection or use of the search-ms: protocol.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence/anti-forensics; final goal is malware execution, data exfiltration, and evasion of detection.

behavioral_signatures: HTML attachments containing <meta http-equiv="refresh"> tags that redirect to search-ms: URIs
HTML links using the search-ms: protocol with remote UNC paths (e.g., \\server\share)
Unusual invocation of Windows Search from browser or email client contexts
Registry modifications that delete or alter the search-ms protocol handler (HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\search-ms)
file_indicators: Zipped email attachments containing HTML files with suspicious naming (e.g., 'INVOICE.html')
HTML files embedding search-ms: URIs in meta refresh or anchor tags
References to remote UNC paths such as \\malicious-server\share within HTML content
network_indicators: Outbound SMB or WebDAV connections to remote servers following the opening of an HTML attachment
Connections to remote shares tunneled through services like Cloudflare or similar proxy/CDN providers
Unexpected SMB/WebDAV traffic originating from email client or browser processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor inbound email attachments for zipped HTML files containing search-ms: URIs, especially those referencing remote UNC paths. Alert on <meta http-equiv="refresh"> tags or anchor tags that redirect to OS-level protocols. Detect registry modifications that delete or alter the search-ms protocol handler. Correlate user actions opening HTML attachments with subsequent SMB/WebDAV network connections to untrusted servers. Flag any invocation of Windows Search from non-standard contexts such as browsers or email clients, and investigate any outbound connections to remote shares immediately following such events.
